record.original_question: Is every element in Diff ∞ + (S ) a commutator?

evidence.quote: Question 7.1. Is every element in Diff ∞ + (S ) a commutator?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $\mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$ denote the group, under composition, of orientation-preserving $C^{\infty}$ diffeomorphisms of the circle $S^{1}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. For $f,g\in \mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$, the commutator is $[f,g]=fgf^{-1}g^{-1}$. Determine whether every element of $\mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$ can be written as a single commutator: that is, given $h\in \mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$, do there always exist $f,g\in \mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$ such that $h=fgf^{-1}g^{-1}$?
artifact.status_search_result: It is classical (Herman, Thurston, Mather) that $\mathrm{Diff}^{\infty}_{+}(S^{1})$ is simple and uniformly perfect: every element is a product of a bounded number of commutators (in fact at most a small constant, with results showing four commutators suffice in a neighborhood of the identity). However, whether every element is expressible as a single commutator appears not to be established in the literature; standard fragmentation/perfectness arguments do not yield commutator length one. No source found resolving this specific question.

status_evidence.title: A short proof that Diff_c(M) is perfect — Kathryn Mann
status_evidence.snippet: Any diffeomorphism g near the identity can be written as a product of four commutators g = [g_1,f_1]...[g_4,f_4].
status_evidence.claim: Diff_+(S^1) is uniformly perfect with commutator length at most 4 near the identity, but single-commutator expressibility is not established.

status_evidence.title: Uniform perfectness of diffeomorphism groups, I — MPIM
status_evidence.snippet: D(M) is uniformly perfect if dim(M) is not 2 or 4.
status_evidence.claim: Uniform perfectness is known, but the question of commutator length exactly 1 for Diff_+(S^1) is a stronger open question.
